q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way in which the alliance system contributed to the outbreak of World War I.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the assassination at Sarajevo led to a continental war rather than a localized conflict, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which nationalism increased tensions among European powers before 1914.

sample_answers.a: The rigid alliance blocs (Triple Entente vs. Triple Alliance) meant that a dispute between Austria-Hungary and Serbia automatically pulled in Russia, Germany, France, and Britain through binding mobilization commitments, turning a Balkan crisis into a European war.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, the alliance system functioned as a transmission belt: Austria-Hungary's attack on Serbia triggered Russia's mobilization, which triggered Germany's war plans against both Russia and France, so each power's defensive commitments escalated the crisis step by step.
sample_answers.c: Serbian nationalism sought to unite South Slavs at Austria-Hungary's expense, while German and French nationalists demanded military strength and revenge for past defeats; these competing nationalisms made governments unwilling to compromise and eager to prove their resolve.

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain the outbreak of World War I as the result of a dangerous combination: rigid alliance commitments, military plans that rewarded striking first, and nationalist pressures that made compromise politically costly. The alliance system did not make war inevitable, but it ensured that once Austria-Hungary decided to punish Serbia for the Sarajevo assassination, the crisis could not remain localized. Russia mobilized to defend Serbia, Germany implemented its long-prepared plan for a two-front war, and France and Britain were drawn in by their own commitments. Each government believed it was acting defensively, yet each step of mobilization — which military planners treated as equivalent to war — narrowed the options for peace until the great powers had talked and mobilized themselves into a catastrophe none had fully intended.
—Historian's account of the causes of World War I in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE demand Austria-Hungary makes of Serbia in the ultimatum.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which the terms of the ultimatum made war more likely.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Austria-Hungary issued such severe demands in July 1914.

sample_answers.a: Austria-Hungary demands that Serbia allow Austro-Hungarian officials to participate in the investigation of the Sarajevo assassination on Serbian territory — a direct infringement of Serbian sovereignty.
sample_answers.b: The demands were deliberately written to be unacceptable: no sovereign state could admit foreign officials to conduct investigations within its borders, so Serbia's partial rejection gave Austria-Hungary a pretext for war.
sample_answers.c: Austro-Hungarian leaders, assured of German backing, wanted to crush Serbian nationalism once and for all and believed a swift, localized war would restore the empire's prestige before Russia could intervene.

q2.stimulus:
The Royal Serbian Government shall suppress any publication which incites to hatred and contempt of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy. It shall dissolve the society styled Narodna Odbrana and all other societies engaged in propaganda against Austria-Hungary. It shall remove from military service and from the administration all officers and officials guilty of propaganda against Austria-Hungary. It shall accept the collaboration in Serbia of representatives of the Austro-Hungarian Government in the suppression of the subversive movement. The Royal Serbian Government has forty-eight hours to reply.
—Adapted from the Austro-Hungarian ultimatum to Serbia, 23 July 1914

q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE pattern shown on the map regarding European alliances in 1914.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the alliance blocs shown on the map shaped military planning before World War I.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Italy's position in the alliance system proved unstable after 1914.

sample_answers.a: Europe is divided into two armed camps: the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain) facing the Triple Alliance/Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy), with the alliances geographically interlocked so that each bloc confronted the other on multiple frontiers.
sample_answers.b: Germany's central position between France and Russia led to the Schlieffen Plan, which assumed a two-front war and required striking France first through Belgium; the map's geography made German planners believe speed and preemption were essential.
sample_answers.c: Italy had joined the Triple Alliance for protection against France, but its real rivalries were with Austria-Hungary over territory; when war came, Italy declared neutrality and in 1915 joined the Entente, which promised it Austrian lands — showing the alliances were marriages of convenience.

q3.stimulus: The map shows Europe in 1914 divided into alliance blocs: the Triple Entente (France, Russia, and Great Britain, with Serbia and Belgium aligned) facing the Central Powers of the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy). The map makes visible how the two blocs confronted each other across multiple borders, with Germany positioned between France to the west and Russia to the east.
